column1: Why do metrics, logs, and traces form a 'complete basis set' for observability?
column2: They decompose system behavior into three orthogonal dimensions: quantitative trends (metrics), qualitative context (logs), and causal topology (traces) — none of which the others can independently reconstruct.

column1: How does Datadog's agent-based collection model invert traditional polling architecture?
column2: Instead of centralized scrapers polling service endpoints, Datadog deploys lightweight agents (sidecars/DaemonSets) that continuously push telemetry to regional intake endpoints via persistent HTTP/2 connections.

column1: What are the three phases of Datadog's deterministic query evaluation pipeline for metrics?
column2: 1) Temporal rollup (collapses high-resolution samples within time windows), 2) Space aggregation (collapses multiple tag-differentiated series via sum/avg/max/percentile), 3) Arithmetic/boolean operations combining post-aggregation series.

column1: Why does the order of temporal rollup vs. space aggregation matter in Datadog metric queries?
column2: It determines whether you compute the 'average of maximums' or the 'maximum of averages' — these produce radically different signals when aggregating across many heterogeneous hosts.

column1: What distinguishes a gauge metric from a count/rate metric in Datadog's type system?
column2: A gauge represents instantaneous sampled state (e.g., CPU %), while a count/rate accumulates monotonically and only conveys meaning through its rate of change — each has a distinct aggregation contract.

column1: In Datadog APM, what structural invariant must a reconstructed trace graph preserve?
column2: Causality preservation: if span A causally precedes span B in execution, the parent-pointer chain in the reconstructed trace must reflect that ordering, even if spans arrive out of order.

column1: What identifiers does a Datadog APM span carry to enable trace reconstruction?
column2: A trace identifier (shared across the whole distributed transaction) and a span identifier plus a parent span reference, forming a tree rooted at the originating service.

column1: What is the fundamental tradeoff underlying all alerting threshold configuration?
column2: Sensitivity vs. specificity (from signal detection theory): a perfectly sensitive monitor fires on every real problem, a perfectly specific one never false-fires — these properties directly conflict.

column1: What is Datadog's default monitor evaluation cycle, and what does it compute each cycle?
column2: 60 seconds; each cycle retrieves the metric time-series for the configured query window, applies an aggregation function (avg/max/min/sum), and produces a single scalar tested against thresholds.

column1: What is the 'aliasing problem' in Datadog monitor evaluation?
column2: A transient spike (e.g., lasting 90 seconds) may fail to register as a threshold crossing if it falls between two evaluation window boundaries, since alerts fire only at discrete evaluation ticks, not instantaneously.

column1: In Datadog's distributed agent architecture, what is the role of the system-probe process?
column2: A privileged sidecar process that uses eBPF programs to capture network flows and security events directly at the kernel level.

column1: What distinct roles do the core agent, trace agent, and process agent play in Datadog's architecture?
column2: Core agent: collects infra metrics via checks and talks to the backend. Trace agent: receives APM spans, samples/aggregates, forwards traces. Process agent: collects live process tables and container metadata.
